title: Two missed Olympics, two devastating injuries, one world title: Skye Blakely’s long road back | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Skye Blakely is doing something incredibly daring these days. She is dreaming.

Even more, she is dreaming without limits. Not just considering what she might accomplish but thinking beyond the edges of possibility and wondering how much she can achieve.

“It feels like being little again,” Blakely tells CNN Sportsof her new approach. “There are no limits to what you dream when you’re a child, right? You see someone, a role model, and you just say, ‘I want to do that. This is what I’m going to do when I’m big.’ That’s how I feel, like I’m six or seven again.”

Blakely is not exactly wizened. She is all of 21 years old. Hers, however, are 21 years lined with scar tissue, both literal and figurative.

Two cataclysmic injuries – atorn ulnar collateral ligamentin her elbow that requiredTommy Johnsurgery and a torn Achilles tendon – robbed Blakely first of her opportunities, then of her innocence and finally of her confidence. Twice unable to vie for a spot on the Olympic team, she struggled through the physical toll of recovery and the mental anguish of uncertainty, worried the path she long envisioned for herself had been blocked for good.

Now finally and firmly on the other side of it all, Blakely won the all-around world championship crown in October, becoming the ninth American woman to do so and the first since Simone Biles in 2023. The gold medal around her neck has been known to act as its own albatross, foisting upon its bearer the title of next gymnastics darling. And, though we are still two years out from the Los Angeles Games, it is never too early to ease the Olympic hype train out of the station.

As Jordan Chiles and Sunisa Lee work on comebacks and Simone Biles remains mum about her future, it is Blakely who – at least for now – emerges as the brightest hope for Team USA. The world crown only reaffirmed it.

Yet Blakely comes at the inevitable maelstrom with a unique one-two punch: The steely reserve borne out of the loneliness of recovery, and the wide-eyed joy reawakened from time off. Her misfortune – it turns out – might be her superpower.

“I don’t want to say I needed it,” Blakely says. “I definitely didn’t, but it shaped me and it changed me.”

To be certain, Blakely planned and thought she was on a linear path. A talented gymnast who toddled after her big sister, Sloane, into the sport, Blakely was seven when she watched Gabby Douglas capture Olympic all-around gold in London in 2012. She decided she wanted to do that, blissfully unaware that Douglas had just joined a small sisterhood of what was then just four American women.

Improbably, Blakely actually had the big skills to match her big dreams, making her first national team in 2018 and her senior debut in 2021.

The reshuffling of the Olympic deck brought on by the Covid-19 pandemic opened an unexpected door for Blakely. Had the Games been held as scheduled, the 15-year-old Blakely would have been too young to compete. The one-year delay, however, changed everything and Blakely headed to the US Olympic trials in St. Louis, hoping to earn a place at the Tokyo Games. During warmups on vault, her first apparatus, her arm gave way as she ruptured the UCL in her elbow, necessitating surgery and a seven-month recovery.

Still, Blakely was young, with plenty of opportunities ahead of her. By 2022, she was on the US team at worlds and, in 2024, slotted herself behind Biles as the team’s best all-arounder at nationals, seemingly a shoo-in for the Paris Games.

During the Wednesday practice before the trials officially began, Blakely’s right leg gave way as she practiced a floor routine pass. Coaches carried her off the floor and Blakely left the arena in a wheelchair, officials confirming the next day she had torn her Achilles.

“I thought I saw low in 2021, but 2024 was truly different,” Blakely said. “The goal was so close, so for it to happen a second time, that low was so much worse. I kept asking myself, ‘How are we back here again?’”

Achilles recovery is brutal for anyone, but especially cruel for an athlete accustomed to relying on her lower body for strength and power.

“My brain definitely lost confidence in my foot,” Blakely said.

Even worse, she lost confidence in herself. Friends and family tried to boost Blakely’s spirits, reminding her that she’d been through hard times before with the elbow injury. But devastated by the double whammy, she took their good intentions and twisted them around, turning the “Yes you can” into “Why me?”

Post injury, Blakely followed through on her intention to enroll at the University of Florida. She’d committed to the Gators two years prior, planning to join the team after Paris.

Blakely initially viewed it as just a checked box on the to-do list but soon found that the relocation and change of scenery was just what she needed.

Access to the Gators’ physical therapy and athletic training services immediately buoyed her recovery, but it was the mental solace Blakely found in the Gator community that truly changed everything. In a cruel twist of irony, her teammate Kayla DiCello suffered the exact same injury during the exact same trials meet, giving Blakely’s misery the company it needed.

The two muddled through the drudgery of recovery together but also celebrated even the smallest of victories – the first day out of the boot, jumping on one leg, walking without a limp. It gave Blakely the one thing she’d been missing.

“There are so many what ifs and just doubts because the recovery wasn’t easy,” she said. “I struggled some days but being able to celebrate even the smallest thing, it let me hold on to that tiny, tiny, tiny bit of hope.”

She competed solely on the uneven bars during her freshman season – the least demanding apparatus for her Achilles. A mere 199 days after the injury, she competed again, earning a 9.725, and hit for a 9.925 in the NCAA regional final.

Over the summer, she slowly and methodically worked her way back, increasing her strength as well as her confidence. She added balance beam and floor exercise to her collegiate repertoire to start the 2026 season, before diving back into all-around in February of that year.

When she headed to the US championships in August, Blakely finally felt like she was on the right track.

Instead, after finishing tied for the lead at the end of day one, she stumbled in the second-day rotation, dropping to a seventh-place finish. The rational part of her mind understood that she was just a few months into international all-around training but the other part – the one that fought through the doubts since 2021 – wondered if this was it, if her best wasn’t going to be good enough again.

Not long after, while visiting Los Angeles for an event, Blakely found herself alone in a hotel room with her thoughts and her demons. She put pen to paper and wrote out a detailed week-by-week workout plan. The schedule in and of itself wasn’t anything extraordinary; it was the act of doing, of taking ownership of her future, that mattered.

“It was telling myself there is no other option,” Blakely said. “This is your plan. This is what you’re going to work for. Shake off the defeat and lack of motivation just because you’re frustrated or you feel bummed and dig deep and go be Skye Blakely.”

Being Skye Blakely, she finally realized, wasn’t measurable. No score, no hit routine, no medal would determine her worth. It was far bigger than that.

“Take risks, be in the moment,” she said. “Just dream like you’re a little kid again.”

At worlds in Rotterdam, Blakely entered the finals in second before opening with a 14.200 on vault, the second-highest score in the final. She followed that with a 14.400 on bars and 14.200 on beam, both third-best, before heading to floor.

When she finished, Blakely thrust her right arm up as the final note of the music faded and the dam broke. Her lips quivering as the years’ worth of stored-up tears finally arrived, Blakely put that same right hand across her heart, trying to simultaneously contain and embrace her emotions.

She did not yet know her score on floor. She did not know, for certain, that she had just won the all-around title at the world championships.

That would come in due time, bringing with it another round of triumphant tears.

In that nanosecond after she finished her routine, all Blakely knew was that she had just completed a mistake-free, injury-free four rotations of gymnastics on one of the sport’s biggest stages.

And it was enough.

Actually, it was everything.
